strengths: Addresses a highly relevant and practical challenge in simulation-based inference (SBI): the prohibitive computational cost of high-fidelity scientific simulators.

Proposes a simple, intuitive, and effective transfer learning strategy (MF-NPE) that leverages existing cheap, low-fidelity models to pre-train density estimators before fine-tuning on limited high-fidelity data.

Successfully handles differences in parameter dimensionality between low- and high-fidelity simulators using a dummy variable pre-training approach, which is shown to naturally fall back to the prior.
Extends the framework to sequential neural posterior estimation (MF-TSNPE) and active learning (A-MF-TSNPE) to target informative high-fidelity simulations.

The evaluation on real-world biophysical tasks (a multicompartmental neuron model and a plastic spiking network) is excellent. It uses well-established low-fidelity approximations (single-compartment and mean-field models) and shows substantial savings in high-fidelity simulation budget (up to two orders of magnitude).
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is somewhat incremental, as pre-training via weight initialization and active learning with posterior variance ensembles are established techniques in deep learning and SBI, though their combination in this multifidelity setup is highly effective and well-executed.

The success of the method depends heavily on the quality and availability of a suitable low-fidelity model. The paper lacks a systematic study or discussion on what happens when the low-fidelity simulator is severely misspecified or fundamentally inconsistent with the high-fidelity model, which could potentially cause negative transfer.

The active learning variant (A-MF-TSNPE) yields very marginal improvements over MF-TSNPE while incurring significantly higher computational overhead due to training ensembles, making its practical utility somewhat limited.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly important and practical bottleneck in simulation-based inference (SBI): the prohibitive computational cost of running high-fidelity simulators.
The proposed MF-NPE framework is intuitive and elegantly combines transfer learning (pre-training on cheap low-fidelity simulations) with neural density estimators.
The method successfully handles cases with mismatched parameter dimensionalities between low- and high-fidelity models, which is a common scenario in real-world applications.

The evaluation is exceptionally strong, covering a statistical task with analytical ground truth and two highly complex, computationally demanding neuroscience tasks (a multicompartmental neuron model and a recurrent plastic spiking network).

The empirical results demonstrate outstanding sample efficiency, achieving comparable or superior posterior estimates using up to two orders of magnitude fewer high-fidelity simulations than standard NPE.
The paper is exceptionally well-written, with high-quality figures, clear algorithmic pseudocode, and thorough appendices detailing the experimental setups.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution (transfer learning via pre-training and fine-tuning) is conceptually straightforward, offering limited novelty from a machine learning perspective.
The treatment of exclusive high-fidelity parameters during low-fidelity pre-training as dummy variables is relatively simplistic, and more advanced network adaptation strategies are not explored.
The active learning extension (A-MF-TSNPE) provides only marginal performance gains while being computationally expensive and difficult to tune, as acknowledged by the authors.

The performance of the method highly relies on the quality of the low-fidelity model, but the paper lacks a systematic sensitivity analysis or discussion on how severe model discrepancy or a poor low-fidelity model might impact the final posterior (e.g., risk of getting stuck in bad local minima during fine-tuning).

strengths: Addresses a highly relevant and practical bottleneck in simulation-based inference (SBI), namely the prohibitive computational cost of high-fidelity simulators.

The evaluation focuses on complex, high-dimensional neuroscience applications (such as a multicompartmental neuron model and a 24-dimensional plastic spiking neural network) rather than just simple toy problems.
Shows strong empirical efficiency in terms of the number of high-fidelity simulations required, achieving comparable posterior estimations with up to two orders of magnitude fewer runs.
The paper is well-structured, clearly written, and provides comprehensive details about the simulator configurations and experimental setups in the appendix.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is quite limited. The core idea relies on standard pre-training and fine-tuning (transfer learning) applied directly to normalizing flows, without introducing any new theoretical insights or specialized architectural designs to handle the discrepancy between fidelities.

The handling of parameter space dimensionality mismatch is heuristically addressed using 'dummy variables'. If the low-fidelity model lacks half of the parameters (e.g., 12 vs 24 parameters in the spiking network), the pre-trained flow only learns the prior for the missing parameters. When fine-tuning on a very small high-fidelity budget (e.g., 50 to 100 samples), it is unclear how the flow can accurately learn the complex high-dimensional correlations and dependencies involving these newly active parameters.

There is a lack of a comprehensive wall-clock time or holistic computational cost-benefit analysis. Pre-training on $10^4$ to $10^5$ low-fidelity simulations and training the normalizing flow on this large dataset incurs non-trivial computational overhead. Without comparing the total training and simulation time (LF + HF vs. HF only), it is hard to assess whether the proposed method actually saves overall compute resources, especially if the LF simulator or the flow training is slow.

The active learning variant (A-MF-TSNPE) introduces significant computational complexity (requiring training an ensemble of neural density estimators) yet provides only 'minor improvements' over MF-TSNPE, making its practical value questionable.
The empirical evaluation lacks comparison with other potential multifidelity or surrogate-assisted SBI methods, comparing only against standard single-fidelity NPE/TSNPE baselines.

strengths: Highly relevant and impactful topic: addresses the high computational cost of simulation-based inference (SBI) by leveraging cheap low-fidelity simulators.

Strong empirical evaluation across a diverse set of tasks, including standard benchmarks and two realistic, computationally expensive neuroscience applications (multicompartment neuron and recurrent spiking network).

Intuitive and flexible methodology: the transfer learning framework easily accommodates multiple fidelity levels and cases where the low-fidelity simulator uses fewer parameters than the high-fidelity one.
Helpful analysis of transfer learning dynamics: explores and identifies mutual information and representational coherence as key factors in determining when pre-training is effective.
Excellent clarity and reproducibility, with detailed descriptions of hyperparameters, architectures, and computational costs in the appendix.
weaknesses: The core transfer learning approach (simple fine-tuning) is quite straightforward, representing a relatively incremental methodological advancement, though highly practical.

The active learning variant (A-MF-TSNPE) introduces significant computational overhead because it requires training an ensemble of density estimators, which limits its usefulness to cases where simulations are exceptionally expensive.

A-MF-TSNPE uses a heuristically mixed proposal (proposal samples + active samples) without proposal correction, which theoretically biases the posterior estimate, though the authors attempt to mitigate this by keeping the active portion small.

strengths: Addresses a highly practical and significant bottleneck in simulation-based inference (SBI): the extreme computational cost associated with running high-fidelity scientific simulators.

Provides an exceptionally thorough and diverse empirical evaluation, testing the approach across four standard benchmarks (SIR, SLCP, OUprocess, Gaussian Blob) and two highly realistic, complex neuroscience simulators (a multicompartment neuron model and a recurrent spiking network with 24 parameters).

Offers valuable empirical insights into when transfer learning helps (Section 4.4 and Appendix B) by investigating the role of mutual information and representational coherence between the low-fidelity and high-fidelity models.
The paper is very well-written, clear, and includes an extensive appendix with detailed computational cost tables, training procedures, and robustness checks, indicating high reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty of MF-NPE is somewhat limited. Pre-training a neural density estimator on a large dataset of cheap simulations and fine-tuning it on a smaller target dataset of expensive simulations is a standard deep learning transfer strategy, rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic contribution.

The sequential active learning variant (A-MF-TSNPE) introduces an acquisition function to guide simulation placement but lacks a mathematically sound proposal correction. As the authors admit in Appendix M.2, this introduces a bias into the posterior estimation and violates the theoretical guarantees of sequential neural posterior estimation.

While the paper demonstrates massive savings in high-fidelity simulation budgets, it assumes that low-fidelity simulations have negligible computational costs. The pre-training requires substantial amounts of low-fidelity samples ($10^4$ to $10^5$), and the paper lacks a joint resource-allocation framework to balance the budgets of both fidelities optimally.

The active learning variant A-MF-TSNPE does not show consistent improvements over MF-TSNPE in several tasks (such as SLCP and SIR in Figure 2), despite the increased computational burden of maintaining and training an ensemble of density estimators.

strengths: Addresses a highly practical and significant problem: the massive computational bottleneck of simulation-based inference (SBI) when high-fidelity simulators are expensive.
Comprehensive and diverse evaluation across four benchmarks and two highly realistic and challenging neuroscience applications (L5PC biophysical neuron model and Recurrent Spiking Network).

Successfully handles mismatched parameter spaces, showing that the method can easily generalize to settings where the low-fidelity simulator has a subset of the high-fidelity parameters (e.g., 12 vs. 24 parameters in the spiking network).
Provides a very detailed and honest computational cost analysis (Appendix K), detailing the exact wall-clock training vs. simulation time trade-offs.

Includes a thoughtful and rigorous empirical investigation (Section 4.4 and Appendix B) of when pre-training actually helps, introducing concepts of mutual information and representational coherence under systematic perturbations.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is relatively straightforward, as the main approach combines standard fine-tuning of neural density estimators (neural spline flows) with existing sequential (TSNPE) and active learning techniques.

The active learning extension (A-MF-TSNPE) introduces a biased proposal without applying proposal correction (as noted in Appendix M.2). Although the authors mitigate this using a heuristic split ($B = 0.2M$), a more thorough analysis of the resulting posterior calibration and potential approximation errors is missing.

The method assumes that both simulators operate over the same observation domain. While upscaling works for images (Gaussian Blob), in many real-world settings, low-fidelity simulators produce structurally different observations, which might limit naive transfer learning.

The paper would benefit from a more detailed comparison or discussion with the referenced concurrent multifidelity SBI works (e.g., Thiele et al., 2025; Hikida et al., 2025; Saoulis et al., 2025) to better position the proposed transfer-learning framework.
